headline: Did the government lie to a judge about a golf course?
summary: Judge Ana Reyes said Friday she will appoint a special master to find out if government lawyers misled her about Trump's plan for a Washington golf course. Trump said October 18 it would close for 15 months. A government lawyer told the court the next day there was no plan to close it. On October 28 the department admitted there was.

cover_question.q: What happens if you lie to a judge?

cover_answer: A judge finds out. Lawyers who lie can be punished.
table_question: Is it lying if you leave out the part that matters?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Washington there is a golf course that is 106 years old, with hundreds of big trees. The president wants to rebuild it, and some people asked a judge to stop him. The judge thinks the government's lawyers may not have told her the whole truth, so she is checking, like a teacher checking a story. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Telling the truth to the person in charge is a rule a six-year-old already lives under. The golf course is just where it happened.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the trees and the teacher checking a story, and leaves out special masters and appeals. The rule about truth is one they already live under. Expect "Did they lie?" The honest answer is that nobody knows yet, and the judge picked someone to find out.

8-12.script: Trump wants to rebuild a public golf course. He posted it would close for 15 months. The next day a government lawyer told the judge: no plan to close. Then the department admitted there was. Lawyers owe a judge the truth, as players owe the referee, so she is checking.
8-12.why: Kids this age track whether adults follow their own rules. This gap is one they can see.
8-12.why_long: An eight-to-twelve-year-old is testing whether adults apply the rules to themselves, so the script puts the dates in order and lets the gap between the post and the courtroom speak. The referee is the mechanism they know: answer honestly or the game stops. Expect "So what happens to them?" Say that depends on what she finds.

13-17.script: A government lawyer said one thing in court; the president posted the opposite. Which counts? The judge asked a top Justice Department official when he knew. He asked what "involved" meant; she read him the dictionary. What should happen to a lawyer who misled a judge?
13-17.why: Teenagers test whether adults argue honestly. Parsing "involved" is a move they know from their own arguments.
13-17.why_long: A teenager is testing whether adults argue in good faith, so the script leads with the question and lets the dictionary moment land. Two things to hold: the president can change his plans, and his lawyers still owe the court the truth. Expect "Will anything happen?" Say the investigator can question people under oath.

5-7.q: What happens if you lie to a judge?
5-7.a: A judge can punish lawyers who do. This judge isn't sure yet, so she picked someone to read the papers and ask questions. Then she will decide.

8-12.q: Why does a golf course matter so much?
8-12.a: It's 106 years old, open to anyone, and 400 trees are already gone.
An outside investigator the judge picks. They can put people under oath.

13-17.q: Can a judge actually punish the Justice Department?
13-17.a: Lawyers can be sanctioned, held in contempt or referred for charges.

13-17.q: Didn't Trump announce the closure himself?
13-17.a: Yes, on October 18. His lawyers said the next day there was no plan.
